claims.text: The magnetocaloric response of as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEAs is governed by grain-boundary density and the distribution of associated defects.
Hysteresis in these alloys is governed by grain-boundary density and the distribution of associated defects.
Grain boundaries and related defects act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for the first-order magnetostructural transition.
A high density of grain boundaries broadens the magnetic-entropy-change response over a wider temperature interval.
A high density of grain boundaries reduces hysteresis losses.
Reducing the density of grain boundaries will sharpen the magnetostructural transition.
Reducing the density of grain boundaries will increase hysteresis.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal microstructure.
The as-deposited alloy has fine grains and a relatively high grain-boundary and defect density.
A controlled low-temperature anneal can produce measurable grain coarsening and reduce grain-boundary density without changing composition or inducing new phases.
After annealing, the reduced defect density will favor more homogeneous nucleation of the transition.
Annealed samples with coarser grains will exhibit a sharper magnetic-entropy-change peak than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples with coarser grains will exhibit a higher peak magnetic entropy change than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit a larger hysteresis-loop area during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles than the as-deposited baseline.
The as-deposited baseline has a broad, relatively low-hysteresis magnetocaloric response.
The predicted relationships apply near the first-order magnetostructural transition under low applied fields, provided annealing causes grain coarsening without a phase change.
Elastic strain, local compositional inhomogeneity, and annealing-induced changes in chemical ordering may also influence the transition and hysteresis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says reduced defects produce more homogeneous nucleation, but then attributes increased hysteresis to energy-barrier differences becoming more pronounced. More homogeneous nucleation ordinarily implies a narrower barrier distribution, so the stated barrier explanation is internally unclear.
